html:
A treaty signed in London on 17 March 1824 in which Britain and the Netherlands split the Malay world between them along the Strait of Malacca. The line it drew is roughly the border between Malaysia and Indonesia today.

The two powers had quarrelled since the Napoleonic Wars, when Britain held Dutch Java, and more so after Stamford Raffles founded Singapore in 1819 in a region the Dutch claimed. Under the treaty the Dutch gave Britain Malacca and their posts in India and dropped their objection to Singapore. Britain gave the Dutch Bencoolen, its post on Sumatra, and promised to make no settlements south of the Strait of Singapore. Each side kept trading rights in the other's ports.

The result was two colonial worlds: British Malaya, which soon formed the Straits Settlements, and the Dutch East Indies. Peoples who had shared one Malay trading world for centuries ended up in different states. The treaty also promised to respect Aceh, which the Dutch later invaded in 1873.
